# Salesforce CLI to psfdx parity

<!-- Generated by scripts/parity/New-CliParityReport.ps1. Do not edit by hand: change docs/cli-parity-mapping.json and regenerate. -->

This report compares the commands of Salesforce CLI **2.159.7** (the latest stable release when it was generated) with what psfdx actually runs. It is built from the commands the modules pass to sf, not from cmdlet counts or README claims. How to read it and how to regenerate it are at the end.

**Scope.** The plugin set that `sf commands` lists for the CLI version above: the core plugins that ship with it and the just-in-time plugins it installs on first use. Plugins you install yourself are not in scope.

## Summary

| Plugin set | Commands | Wrapped | Partially wrapped | Missing | Deliberately excluded | Not applicable | Covered of in scope |
| :--- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Core plugins (bundled with the CLI) | 214 | 178 | 6 | 12 | 3 | 15 | 93.9% of 196 |
| Just-in-time plugins (installed on first use) | 65 | 26 | 0 | 30 | 0 | 9 | 46.4% of 56 |
| Both | 279 | 204 | 6 | 42 | 3 | 24 | 83.3% of 252 |

"Covered of in scope" is (wrapped + partially wrapped) out of the commands that are neither deliberately excluded nor not applicable. It is only meaningful for the plugin set on its row; a command from a plugin that is not installed is not counted anywhere else.

psfdx exports **256** cmdlets; **225** of them run an sf command themselves. The other **31** are conveniences built on those, or run other programs (npm, Jest) or call the REST API directly, and add no CLI coverage of their own.

**Flags and values.** Across the **210** commands psfdx runs, it passes **1004 of 1018** of their flags (not counting the universal ones listed below). 0 of the flags it does not pass are required by the CLI. For the flags it does pass, **100** have a list of allowed values in the CLI, and psfdx can pass **367 of 373** of those values.

## Covered

Commands psfdx runs, with the cmdlets that run them. "Flags passed" counts the command's flags that some psfdx function passes. "Flags not passed" lists the rest (a flag the CLI requires is marked). "Values not reachable" lists, for a flag that has a list of allowed values in the CLI, the values psfdx cannot pass. Either kind of gap makes a command partially wrapped.

## Flags left out of the per-command view

These flags are on almost every command, so they are not counted against each one. Each is listed once here.

| Flag | psfdx functions that pass it | Commands psfdx runs that have it |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| `--json` | 191 | 198 |
| `--flags-dir` | 0 | 207 |
| `--api-version` | 1 | 150 |

## How to read this

- **Wrapped:** some psfdx function runs the command, passes every one of its flags (apart from `--json`, `--flags-dir` and `--api-version`, which are reported once) and can pass every value the CLI lists for them. **Partially wrapped:** a flag is not passed, or a listed value cannot be passed; both are shown, and a reviewed mapping rule can accept the gap with a reason. Flags are matched by function (the function that builds the command, and the helpers it calls in the same file or in psfdx-shared), so this is a close estimate, not a proof.
- **Values:** the CLI lists the allowed values for some flags (for example `--test-level`). A value is reachable when psfdx writes it literally in the arguments, accepts it through a parameter with a `[ValidateSet()]` (compared without regard to case), or takes the flag's value as free text, in which case any value can be passed. A parameter that is not a `[ValidateSet()]` is free text, even if its help names the values. Flags with no list (names, paths, numbers, query text) are checked for being passed, not for values. The CLI's recorded default counts as reachable only where psfdx can leave the flag out (some code writes it conditionally, or another function that runs the command does not write it); a default the CLI does not record in its command data never counts, so such a value is listed unless the mapping accepts it (`ignoreValues`). A lookup table such as `$map = @{ 'Name' = 'CliValue' }` used as `$map[$x]` after a flag counts as the values for the names a caller can pass for `$x`, followed up the calls. A value that psfdx builds some other way is not followed.
- **Missing:** no psfdx function runs it and nobody has decided why. **Deliberately excluded:** reviewed and left out on purpose, with a reason. **Not applicable:** CLI housekeeping or interactive tooling that a PowerShell wrapper has no use for.
- **One to many, many to one:** a cmdlet can run several commands (a bulk job and its resume), and a command can be run by several cmdlets; both are shown. A cmdlet that only calls other psfdx cmdlets is a convenience and is not counted as coverage.
- **Scope:** the plugin set is what `sf commands` lists for this CLI: the core plugins that ship with it and the just-in-time plugins it installs on first use. Percentages are per plugin set. Plugins you install yourself are not in this report. `Beta` and `preview` commands are counted like the rest and marked.
- **Source of truth:** the commands psfdx runs are read from the code; the reviewed classifications are in `docs/cli-parity-mapping.json`. A new CLI command shows up here as missing; it does not fail the build. A mapping that is invalid does.

## Regenerate

```powershell
./scripts/parity/New-CliParityReport.ps1                      # offline: rebuilds docs/cli-parity.md and .json from the committed inventory
npm install --global @salesforce/cli@latest                  # then, to move to the latest stable CLI:
./scripts/parity/New-CliInventorySnapshot.ps1                # rewrites docs/cli-parity-inventory.json from sf commands --json
./scripts/parity/New-CliParityReport.ps1
```

Only the snapshot step needs the CLI, and none of it needs an org or credentials. A test fails when the committed report does not match the modules, the mapping and the inventory, so regenerate it when you add or change a cmdlet that runs `sf`.
